entries.1:1: God had promised through Jeremiah that the exile would end, and he moved the Persian king Cyrus to act so that promise came true. It shows God keeps his word and can use even a foreign ruler to do it.
entries.1:2: Cyrus credits the God of heaven with giving him his vast empire and says he has been given the job of building God a house in Jerusalem. It reminds the reader that God is over all nations, not just one.
entries.1:3: Cyrus lets any of God's people go back to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple and says God be with them. It shows God making a way for his people to return and worship him again.
entries.1:4: People staying behind in other places are told to help the returning exiles with silver, gold, supplies, and animals for the temple. It shows that those who cannot go can still share in God's work by giving.
entries.1:5: The family leaders of Judah and Benjamin, along with priests and Levites, got ready to go because God stirred their hearts. It shows that real willingness to serve comes from God moving inside a person.
entries.1:6: Their neighbors pitched in with silver and gold articles, supplies, animals, and valuable things, plus freewill offerings. It shows how God provides for his work through the generosity of ordinary people around them.
entries.1:7: Cyrus brought out the temple articles that Nebuchadnezzar had stolen from Jerusalem and put in his own god's temple. It shows God had not forgotten his house, and what was taken would be restored.
entries.1:8: Cyrus had his treasurer Mithredath count out these articles and hand them to Sheshbazzar, the leader of Judah. It shows careful, orderly handling of what was dedicated to God.
entries.1:9: This verse begins listing the exact numbers of the gold and silver articles being returned. It shows the record was kept precisely, so nothing dedicated to God was lost or overlooked.
entries.1:10: The list continues with gold and silver bowls and a thousand other articles. It shows the huge scale of what was being given back for God's house.
entries.1:11: In total 5,400 gold and silver articles were brought back by Sheshbazzar when the exiles returned from Babylon to Jerusalem. It shows God fully restored what had been taken, down to the last item.
entries.2:1: This lists the Jews that the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar had taken captive, and who now came back to their own towns in Jerusalem and Judah. It means God brought his people home after years of exile, and it reminds the reader that God keeps his promises to restore.
entries.2:2: These are the leaders who traveled back with the returning exiles, starting with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. It shows the return was organized under named leaders, and it reminds the reader that God works through ordinary people to carry out his plans.
entries.2:3: This begins a long list of family groups and how many men were in each, starting with the family of Parosh at 2,172. It shows that every returning family was counted and remembered, and it reminds the reader that God values each person and family among his people.
entries.2:4: The family of Shephatiah numbered 372 men. It is one more entry in the record of those who came back, showing that each family group had its place in the return.
entries.2:5: The family of Arah numbered 775 men. The careful counting shows the return was a real, organized event, and it reminds the reader that God knows and keeps track of his people.
entries.2:6: The family of Pahath-moab, through Jeshua and Joab, numbered 2,812 men. This large group shows how many descendants of one family line returned together to rebuild their lives.
entries.2:7: The family of Elam numbered 1,254 men. Each number in this list records real people who made the journey home, showing that God's restoration involved specific, named families.
entries.2:8: The family of Zattu numbered 945 men. The list keeps counting the returning exiles family by family, showing that no group was left out of the record.
entries.2:9: The family of Zaccai numbered 760 men. This is another entry in the census of those who returned, showing the care taken to record who came back.
entries.2:10: The family of Bani numbered 642 men. The record continues, showing that the return involved many different family groups, each with its own place among God's people.
entries.2:11: The family of Bebai numbered 623 men. Each family's number is listed, showing that the returning community was made up of many ordinary households.
entries.2:12: The family of Azgad numbered 1,222 men. The list keeps showing how many people from each family line chose to leave Babylon and return home.
entries.2:13: The family of Adonikam numbered 666 men. This is one more family group counted among those who came back to Judah.
entries.2:14: The family of Bigvai numbered 2,056 men. This was one of the larger family groups in the return, showing how many people from one line made the journey.
entries.2:15: The family of Adin numbered 454 men. The record continues to list each family and its size, showing the return was carefully documented.
entries.2:16: The family of Ater, through Hezekiah, numbered 98 men. Even small family groups are listed, showing that every returning household mattered in the record.
entries.2:17: The family of Bezai numbered 323 men. This is another entry in the list of families who came back from exile to rebuild their homes.
entries.2:18: The family of Jorah numbered 112 men. The list keeps counting the returning families, showing that the community was rebuilt one household at a time.
entries.2:19: The family of Hashum numbered 223 men. Each family's number is recorded, showing the care taken to know who made up the returning people.
entries.2:20: The family of Gibbar numbered 95 men. This small group is still named and counted, showing that no returning family was too small to be remembered.
entries.2:21: The people of Bethlehem numbered 123 men. The list now includes towns as well as families, showing that people returned to specific places to rebuild their communities.
entries.2:22: The men of Netophah numbered 56. This small town's returning men are recorded, showing that even small places had people who came home.
entries.2:23: The men of Anathoth numbered 128. This town's returning men are listed, showing that the return reached many different local communities.
entries.2:24: The people of Azmaveth numbered 42 men. Even a very small group is recorded, showing that every returning community was noted.
entries.2:25: The people of Kiriath-arim, Chephirah, and Beeroth together numbered 743 men. Several nearby towns are grouped together, showing how returning families settled back into their local areas.
entries.2:26: The people of Ramah and Geba together numbered 621 men. These towns' returning people are counted together, showing the return involved whole communities, not just individuals.
entries.2:27: The men of Michmas numbered 122. This town's returning men are recorded, showing that the list covers many small local places.
entries.2:28: The men of Bethel and Ai together numbered 223. These two towns' returning people are counted together, showing that people went back to rebuild in their old home areas.
entries.2:29: The family of Nebo numbered 52 men. This small group is still named, showing that even the smallest returning families were remembered.
entries.2:30: The family of Magbish numbered 156 men. This is another small family group recorded among those who came back from exile.
entries.2:31: The other family of Elam numbered 1,254 men. A second group with the same family name is listed, showing the record was detailed enough to tell apart different branches of a family.
entries.2:32: The family of Harim numbered 320 men. This family group is counted among the returning exiles, adding to the record of who came home.
entries.2:33: The people of Lod, Hadid, and Ono together numbered 725 men. Three towns are grouped together, showing how returning families settled back into their local regions.
entries.2:34: The people of Jericho numbered 345 men. This town's returning people are recorded, showing that the return included people from many different places.
entries.2:35: The family of Senaah numbered 3,630 men. This was one of the largest groups in the return, showing how many people from one family line came back to rebuild.
entries.2:36: This starts a separate list of the priests, beginning with the family of Jedaiah through Jeshua at 973 men. It shows that priests were among the returning exiles, and it reminds the reader that worship and service to God were being restored.
entries.2:37: The priestly family of Immer numbered 1,052 men. The priests are counted separately, showing that the returning community made sure its religious leadership was restored.
entries.2:38: The priestly family of Pashhur numbered 1,247 men. This large priestly group is recorded, showing that many priests returned to serve in the rebuilt temple.
entries.2:39: The priestly family of Harim numbered 1,017 men. The list of priests continues, showing that the returning community carefully organized who would lead worship.
entries.2:40: This lists the Levites, the temple helpers, starting with the family of Jeshua and Kadmiel through Hodaviah at 74 men. It shows that the people who assisted the priests also returned, and it reminds the reader that every role in serving God matters.
entries.2:41: This verse counts the temple musicians who returned from exile, listing 128 descendants of Asaph. It shows that worship through music was an important part of the community's life and was carefully organized.
entries.2:42: This lists the gatekeepers and their families, 139 in all, who were responsible for guarding the temple. It reminds us that even behind-the-scenes jobs mattered in serving God.
entries.2:43: This begins a list of the temple servants, a group who assisted the priests and Levites with practical work. Their inclusion shows that ordinary service was valued alongside more visible roles.
entries.2:44: This continues the list of temple servants by naming more family groups. Each name represents real people who played a part in restoring worship.
entries.2:45: More families of temple servants are named here. The detailed record shows that every worker's contribution was remembered and counted.
entries.2:46: This verse adds more names to the list of temple servants. It shows the community kept careful records of who belonged to which family group.
entries.2:47: The list of temple servant families continues. These were people who supported the work of the temple in practical ways.
entries.2:48: More temple servant families are listed here. Their presence in the record shows they were part of the returning community and its mission.
entries.2:49: This continues naming the families of temple servants. It reflects how the returning exiles were organized by family and role.
entries.2:50: More families of temple servants appear in this verse. The long list shows that many people shared in the support work of the temple.
entries.2:51: The list of temple servant families goes on. Each group had its own identity and place in the community's service.
entries.2:52: This verse names more temple servant families. It shows the record was kept in an orderly way, family by family.
entries.2:53: More families of temple servants are listed. Their work, though less prominent, was part of the community's worship life.
entries.2:54: This closes the list of temple servant families. It shows that even the last names on the list were important enough to be recorded.
entries.2:55: This begins a list of the descendants of Solomon's servants, another group attached to the temple. They were part of the community that returned to rebuild.
entries.2:56: More families of Solomon's servants are named here. The record shows these groups were counted and included in the return.
entries.2:57: This verse adds the final families of Solomon's servants to the list. It shows the community carefully tracked everyone who came back.
entries.2:58: This gives the total number of temple servants and Solomon's servants together, 392. It summarizes the size of this support group in the returning community.
entries.2:59: Some people returned from certain towns but could not prove their family line was Israelite. It shows that belonging to the community was taken seriously and needed evidence.
entries.2:60: This lists the families of those who could not prove their ancestry, 652 people in all. They were still part of the return, even with uncertain records.
entries.2:61: Some priests also could not prove their family line, including one whose ancestor had married into the family of Barzillai. It shows that family identity and records mattered for priestly service.
entries.2:62: When their names could not be found in the family records, these priests were treated as unfit for priestly work. It shows the community applied its rules carefully, even when it was painful.
entries.2:63: The governor told them not to eat the most holy food until a priest could decide their case using the Urim and Thummim. It shows they were not permanently rejected but waited for a proper decision.
entries.2:64: This gives the total number of the whole returning community, 42,360 people. It shows the return from exile was a large, organized movement of people.
entries.2:65: Besides the main group, there were 7,337 servants and 200 musicians. It shows the community included many workers and people who contributed to its life.
entries.2:66: This lists the horses and other transport animals the people brought with them. It shows the return involved real practical needs and resources for the journey and new life.
entries.2:67: This adds camels and donkeys to the count of animals. It shows the community had the livestock needed to travel and settle in the land.
entries.2:68: When some family leaders arrived at the temple site in Jerusalem, they gave freely toward rebuilding God's house. It shows that generosity and commitment to worship were part of the return.
entries.2:69: Each person gave what they could, and the total was a large amount of gold, silver, and priestly robes. It shows that everyone's giving, according to ability, added up to something significant.
entries.2:70: The priests, Levites, musicians, gatekeepers, temple servants, and the rest of the people settled in their own towns. It shows the community was reestablished in the land, each group in its place.
entries.3:1: The Israelites had returned from exile and were living in their own towns, and in the seventh month they all gathered in Jerusalem with one shared purpose. It shows how God's people come together to worship and rebuild, and it invites the reader to join others in seeking God rather than staying isolated.
entries.3:2: The leaders and priests rebuilt the altar for burnt offerings, following what Moses' law had commanded. They started with worship before anything else, showing the reader that putting God first is the right foundation for any new beginning.
entries.3:3: Even though they were afraid of the surrounding peoples, they set the altar in place and offered sacrifices every morning and evening. It means faith can act despite fear, and the reader can keep worshiping and doing what is right even when surrounded by threats.
entries.3:4: They celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles and kept up the daily offerings exactly as the law required. It shows obedience in worship, and it reminds the reader that regular, ordered devotion to God matters, not just occasional big moments.
entries.3:5: After the feast they continued with the regular offerings, new moon offerings, and all the appointed feasts, plus freewill gifts anyone wanted to give. It means worship became a steady habit, and the reader is encouraged to give and worship consistently, not only when they feel like it.
entries.3:6: They began offering sacrifices on the first day of the seventh month, even though the temple foundation had not yet been laid. It shows that worship can start before everything is finished, and the reader can begin honoring God now rather than waiting for perfect conditions.
entries.3:7: They paid workers and supplied food, drink, and oil to the people of Tyre and Sidon so cedar wood could be shipped from Lebanon to Joppa, as King Cyrus had permitted. It shows practical planning and generosity in God's work, and the reader learns that faith involves real effort and resources, not just words.
entries.3:8: In the second year after arriving, the leaders, priests, Levites, and returned exiles began the temple work and put Levites twenty and older in charge of supervising it. It shows organized, shared responsibility in serving God, and the reader sees that everyone has a part to play in building up God's work.
entries.3:9: Jeshua, Kadmiel, Hodaviah's sons, and Henadad's sons with their relatives all worked together to oversee the laborers in God's house. It means teamwork and shared leadership matter, and the reader is encouraged to cooperate with others rather than work alone.
entries.3:10: When the foundation was laid, the priests in their robes with trumpets and the Levites with cymbals praised the Lord, following David's instructions. It shows that milestones in God's work should be marked with praise, and the reader can celebrate and thank God when progress is made.
entries.3:11: They sang back and forth, praising God because he is good and his mercy to Israel lasts forever, and all the people shouted with joy over the foundation. It means God's goodness and lasting mercy deserve loud gratitude, and the reader can trust that his kindness does not run out.
entries.3:12: Many older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the first temple wept loudly when they saw the new foundation, while others shouted for joy. It shows that people can feel deep grief and joy at the same time, and the reader learns to make room for both in others and in themselves.
entries.3:13: The joyful shouting and the weeping mixed together so loudly that the sound carried far away. It means big moments in God's work can stir mixed emotions, and the reader can accept that worship and rebuilding may bring both sorrow and celebration.
entries.4:1: The enemies of the returning Jews heard that they were rebuilding the temple. This shows that doing God's work often attracts opposition from people who don't want it to succeed.
entries.4:2: These opponents offered to help build, claiming they worshiped the same God. But their offer was false, and it reminds us that not everyone who claims to be on our side really is.
entries.4:3: The Jewish leaders refused the offer and said only they would build, as the king had commanded. They were right to protect the work from people whose help would have compromised it.
entries.4:4: The people around them tried to discourage the builders and make them afraid. This shows that opposition can come through fear and discouragement, not just direct attacks.
entries.4:5: They even paid people to work against the Jews and block their plans for years. This reminds us that opposition to good work can be persistent and last a long time.
entries.4:6: Later, under a new king, the enemies formally accused the people of Judah. This shows they kept looking for ways to cause trouble over many years.
entries.4:7: Under another king, a group of officials sent a letter against the Jews in the official language of the region. This was an organized effort to turn the government against God's people.
entries.4:8: Two officials, Rehum and Shimshai, sent their own letter against Jerusalem to the king. This shows how people in power can use their position to oppose God's work.
entries.4:9: The letter came from a whole group of officials and peoples settled in the area. Many voices joined together to accuse the Jews.
entries.4:10: These were the peoples that a great Assyrian king had resettled in Samaria and the region beyond the river. They were outsiders who had been planted there by a foreign empire.
entries.4:11: This is the opening of their letter to King Artaxerxes, identifying themselves as his servants in the province. They presented themselves as loyal subjects while working against the Jews.
entries.4:12: They told the king that the Jews were rebuilding Jerusalem, calling it a rebellious and wicked city, and claimed its walls were nearly finished. This was an exaggerated and hostile report meant to alarm the king.
entries.4:13: They warned that once the city was rebuilt, the Jews would stop paying taxes, which would cost the king money. This was a calculated appeal to the king's financial interests.
entries.4:14: They claimed they were acting out of loyalty to the king and did not want to see him dishonored. This shows how opposition is often dressed up as concern for the ruler's good.
entries.4:15: They asked the king to check his own records, claiming history would show Jerusalem had always been rebellious. This was a selective and misleading use of the past to justify their accusation.
entries.4:16: They warned that if the city was rebuilt, the king would lose control of the whole province. This was the real threat they wanted the king to fear.
entries.4:17: The king sent his reply to the officials and their associates in Samaria and the province. The king had listened to their accusations.
entries.4:18: The king confirmed that he had read and understood their letter. Their accusations had reached the highest authority.
entries.4:19: The king ordered a search, and the records did show that Jerusalem had rebelled against kings in the past. The enemies' claims had enough truth in them to seem convincing.
entries.4:20: The records also showed that powerful kings had once ruled from Jerusalem and collected taxes from the whole region. This made the king nervous about the city's potential.
entries.4:21: The king ordered the work stopped until he gave further permission. The rebuilding was halted by royal command.
entries.4:22: He told them to act carefully and quickly so the problem would not grow. The king was determined to protect his own interests.
entries.4:23: The officials went to Jerusalem at once and forced the Jews to stop building. The opposition succeeded, and the work was halted by force.
entries.4:24: So the rebuilding of God's temple stopped until the second year of King Darius. God's work was paused for a time, but it was not abandoned forever.
entries.5:1: God sent two prophets, Haggai and Zechariah, to encourage the Jews by speaking to them in God's name. It reminds the reader that God speaks to people through faithful messengers to keep them going.
entries.5:2: The leaders Zerubbabel and Jeshua responded by restarting the work on God's temple, and the prophets supported them. It shows that hearing God's word should lead to action, and that God's messengers stand with those who obey.
entries.5:3: A regional governor and his officials came and challenged the Jews, asking who had authorized them to rebuild the temple and its wall. It shows that doing God's work can bring official opposition and hard questions.
entries.5:4: The officials also asked for the names of the men in charge of the building work. It shows that those who oppose God's work often want to identify and target its leaders.
entries.5:5: God was watching over the Jewish leaders, so the work was not stopped while the matter was sent to King Darius for a decision. It reminds the reader that God protects his people and his work even when authorities must be consulted.
entries.5:6: This verse introduces the official letter that the governor and his associates sent to King Darius. It shows that the challenge to the building was handled through proper channels rather than by force.
entries.5:7: The letter opens with a respectful greeting of peace to King Darius. It shows that God's people can deal honestly and respectfully with governing authorities.
entries.5:8: The officials reported that they had visited Judah and found the temple being rebuilt with large stones and timber, and the work was progressing well. It shows that even outsiders could see the serious effort being made.
entries.5:9: The officials told the king they had asked the builders who had given them authority to rebuild. It shows they were investigating whether the work was legally permitted.
entries.5:10: They also asked for the leaders' names so they could report them to the king. It shows the matter was being documented and passed up to the highest authority.
entries.5:11: The Jews answered that they served the God of heaven and earth and were rebuilding the temple that a great king of Israel had built long ago. It shows they were honest about their identity and their historic right to build.
entries.5:12: They explained that their ancestors had angered God, so he allowed Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon to destroy the temple and take the people captive. It shows that they accepted their past failure as the reason for their trouble.
entries.5:13: They noted that King Cyrus of Babylon had issued an order to rebuild God's temple. It shows that the current work was backed by a previous royal decree.
entries.5:14: Cyrus had taken back the gold and silver temple articles that Nebuchadnezzar had seized and given them to Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed as governor. It shows that God can use even pagan kings to restore what was lost.
entries.5:15: Cyrus instructed Sheshbazzar to take the articles to Jerusalem and rebuild God's temple on its original site. It shows the king's order was specific and honored the temple's proper place.
entries.5:16: Sheshbazzar laid the temple foundations in Jerusalem, and the work had continued from then until now, though not yet finished. It shows the rebuilding was a long, ongoing effort rather than a quick success.
entries.5:17: The officials asked the king to search the royal records in Babylon to confirm Cyrus's order and then tell them his decision. It shows that verifying the facts and waiting for proper authority is a wise way to handle opposition.
entries.6:1: King Darius ordered a search of the royal records kept in Babylon to find the original decree. It shows that official records were checked to settle a dispute fairly.
entries.6:2: The search turned up a scroll in the king's palace at Achmetha in Media, and it contained an official written record. This means the evidence they needed was found and written down.
entries.6:3: The scroll recorded that King Cyrus had ordered the temple in Jerusalem to be rebuilt, with its foundations laid and set dimensions. It confirmed the Jews had royal permission to rebuild.
entries.6:4: The decree specified the building materials and said the cost would be paid from the king's treasury. This meant the project had official financial backing.
entries.6:5: Cyrus also ordered that the gold and silver temple items taken by Nebuchadnezzar be returned to their proper place in Jerusalem. This corrected an old wrong and restored what had been taken.
entries.6:6: Darius told the regional officials to stay away from the building site and stop interfering. It means the opponents of the Jews were ordered to back off.
entries.6:7: The officials were told to let the temple work continue and not hinder the Jewish leaders. This gave the builders freedom to keep going.
entries.6:8: Darius ordered that the building costs be paid from royal tax money collected in the region, given promptly so the work would not stop. It meant the project was funded and protected by the king.
entries.6:9: Whatever the priests needed for sacrifices—animals, grain, salt, wine, and oil—was to be supplied every day without fail. This ensured worship could continue regularly.
entries.6:10: The supplies were so the priests could offer sacrifices and pray for the king and his sons. It shows the king wanted the blessing of prayers on his behalf.
entries.6:11: Darius set a harsh penalty for anyone who changed his order: their house would be destroyed and they would be punished severely. It shows how seriously the king protected the decree.
entries.6:12: Darius called on God, who had chosen Jerusalem for his name, to destroy any king or people who tried to alter the order or harm the temple. It placed the project under God's protection as well as the king's.
entries.6:13: The regional officials obeyed Darius's order and carried it out carefully. It shows the opposition stopped once the king's command was clear.
entries.6:14: The Jewish leaders kept building and succeeded, encouraged by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, until the work was finished as God had said and the kings had ordered. It shows God's word and human authority working together.
entries.6:15: The temple was completed on the third day of the month Adar in the sixth year of Darius's reign. It marks the finish of a long, hard rebuilding project.
entries.6:16: The returned Israelites, priests, and Levites celebrated the dedication of the temple with joy. It was a happy moment of thanksgiving for what God had allowed them to finish.
entries.6:17: At the dedication they offered hundreds of animals, plus twelve male goats as a sin offering for all Israel, one for each tribe. It showed they were asking forgiveness and giving thanks for the whole nation.
entries.6:18: They organized the priests and Levites into their assigned groups for temple worship, following what was written in the book of Moses. It means worship was set up again in an orderly way.
entries.6:19: The returned people celebrated Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. It was a key festival remembering how God had rescued them.
entries.6:20: The priests and Levites had all purified themselves, so they were able to kill the Passover lamb for everyone who had returned, including the priests. It shows careful preparation for worship.
entries.6:21: The returned Israelites, along with others who had turned from the sinful ways of the surrounding peoples to serve the Lord, ate the Passover meal together. It shows that anyone willing to follow God could join the community.
entries.6:22: They celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with joy, because the Lord had made the king favorable to them and helped them with the temple work. It reminds the reader that God can move even powerful rulers to help his people.
entries.7:1: This introduces Ezra and traces his family line back through important priests. It shows the reader that Ezra came from a respected priestly heritage.
entries.7:2: The family list continues, linking Ezra to well-known priestly ancestors. It reminds the reader that Ezra's background was rooted in Israel's worship tradition.
entries.7:3: More names in Ezra's family tree are given. Each name connects him further back to the established priesthood.
entries.7:4: The list keeps going, showing an unbroken line of ancestors. This matters because it proves Ezra's right to serve as a priest.
entries.7:5: The family line ends with Aaron, the first high priest. This confirms that Ezra was a genuine descendant of Israel's original priesthood.
entries.7:6: Ezra traveled from Babylon and was highly skilled in God's law, and the king granted his requests because God was with him. It shows the reader that God can open doors through powerful people when he is at work.
entries.7:7: A group of Israelites, including priests, temple workers, and singers, went with Ezra to Jerusalem. It shows that this was a community effort, not just one man's journey.
entries.7:8: Ezra arrived in Jerusalem in the fifth month of the king's seventh year. It simply marks the timing of his arrival.
entries.7:9: The trip from Babylon took about four months, and Ezra made it safely because God helped him. It encourages the reader that God can guide and protect long, difficult journeys.
entries.7:10: Ezra committed himself to studying God's law, obeying it, and then teaching it to others. It gives the reader a model: learn God's word, live it out, then share it.
entries.7:11: This begins a copy of the official letter King Artaxerxes gave Ezra. It shows that Ezra's mission had royal backing.
entries.7:12: The king addresses Ezra with a grand title and wishes him peace. It shows how highly the king regarded Ezra and his God.
entries.7:13: The king decreed that any Israelite in his kingdom who wanted to go to Jerusalem with Ezra was free to do so. It shows the reader that God can move even foreign rulers to support his people.
entries.7:14: The king and his advisors sent Ezra to investigate how things were in Judah and Jerusalem according to God's law. It shows that Ezra's task was to check and guide the community by God's standards.
entries.7:15: Ezra was to carry silver and gold given by the king and his advisors as offerings to Israel's God in Jerusalem. It shows that even outsiders contributed to God's work.
entries.7:16: He was also to collect additional gifts from the people and priests in Babylon for God's temple. It reminds the reader that giving toward God's work came from many sources.
entries.7:17: The money was to be used carefully to buy animals and offerings for the temple altar. It shows the reader that resources given to God should be used purposefully and honestly.
entries.7:18: Ezra and his companions could decide how to use the remaining money as long as it honored God. It shows that God gives freedom in how we manage resources, guided by what pleases him.
entries.7:19: The temple items entrusted to Ezra were to be delivered to God's house in Jerusalem. It reminds the reader to handle what has been dedicated to God with care.
entries.7:20: Any further needs for the temple could be paid from the king's treasury. It shows that God can provide for his work through unexpected sources.
entries.7:21: The king ordered all his treasurers to supply whatever Ezra needed without delay. It shows the reader that God can command widespread cooperation for his purposes.
entries.7:22: The king set generous limits on silver, grain, wine, oil, and unlimited salt for the temple. It shows that God's work was given abundant provision.
entries.7:23: The king insisted that everything God required be done fully, so that trouble would not come on his kingdom. It shows the reader that honoring God brings blessing, while neglecting him brings risk.
entries.7:24: Temple workers were exempted from taxes and fees. It shows that the king wanted those serving God to be free to do their work.
entries.7:25: Ezra was to appoint judges and teach God's laws to those who did not know them. It reminds the reader that leadership and teaching go together in guiding people rightly.
entries.7:26: Anyone who disobeyed God's law or the king's law faced serious punishment. It shows the reader that living under God's authority has real consequences.
entries.7:27: Ezra praised God for moving the king to honor the temple in Jerusalem. It encourages the reader to thank God when he stirs people to support his work.
entries.7:28: Ezra recognized that God's kindness before the king gave him strength, and he gathered leaders to go with him. It shows the reader that God's help can embolden us to lead and act.
entries.8:1: This begins a list of the family leaders who traveled back to Jerusalem from Babylon with Ezra, during the reign of King Artaxerxes. It reminds the reader that this return was a real, organized journey led by named people.
entries.8:2: This continues the list, naming specific men from important priestly and royal family lines who made the trip. It shows that people from Israel's most significant families were part of the return.
entries.8:3: Here the list names Zechariah from the family of Parosh, along with 150 men traveling with him. It shows the group was made up of whole family groups, not just individuals.
entries.8:4: This names Eliehoenai from the family of Pahath-moab, who brought 200 men with him. Each entry shows how the returning community was counted family by family.
entries.8:5: This lists another group of 300 men traveling under a leader from the family of Shecaniah. It continues the careful record of who was making the journey.
entries.8:6: Ebed from the family of Adin is named here with 50 men. Even the smaller groups were recorded, showing that every family mattered in the return.
entries.8:7: Jeshaiah from the family of Elam is listed with 70 men. The record keeps showing that the returning group was made up of many different families.
entries.8:8: Zebadiah from the family of Shephatiah is named with 80 men. The list continues to document each family's contribution to the journey.
entries.8:9: Obadiah from the family of Joab is listed with 218 men. This larger group shows that some families sent many people back to Jerusalem.
entries.8:10: A leader from the family of Shelomith is named with 160 men. The list keeps counting the people who committed to the return.
entries.8:11: Zechariah from the family of Bebai is listed with only 28 men. Even a small group is included, showing that no one was overlooked.
entries.8:12: Johanan from the family of Azgad is named with 110 men. The record continues to show the size and makeup of each family group.
entries.8:13: The last sons of Adonikam are named here with 60 men. This shows that even the remaining members of a family were included in the return.
entries.8:14: Uthai and Zabbud from the family of Bigvai are listed with 70 men. This ends the list of families who traveled back with Ezra.
entries.8:15: Ezra gathered the people by a river and camped there for three days, then noticed that no Levites had come. This matters because Levites were needed to serve in the temple.
entries.8:16: Ezra sent for a group of respected and wise leaders to help solve the problem of the missing Levites. It shows he acted carefully by involving capable men.
entries.8:17: Ezra sent these leaders to Iddo, a chief in Casiphia, asking him to send temple workers to join them. It shows Ezra actively recruiting the people needed for God's house.
entries.8:18: With God's help, the group brought back a Levite named Ish-sechel along with Sherebiah and his relatives, eighteen men in all. It shows that their effort to find temple workers succeeded because God helped them.
entries.8:19: Hashabiah and Jeshaiah from the family of Merari are named with twenty of their relatives and sons. This adds more Levites to the group needed for temple service.
entries.8:20: They also brought 220 temple servants, whose families had long been assigned to help the Levites. These workers were all listed by name, showing they were valued and organized.
entries.8:21: Ezra called for a time of fasting and prayer by the river, asking God to guide them and protect their families and belongings on the journey. It shows they depended on God rather than on their own strength.
entries.8:22: Ezra had told the king that God protects his servants, so he was ashamed to ask for soldiers to guard them. He chose to trust God's protection instead of looking inconsistent about his faith.
entries.8:23: So they fasted and prayed, and God answered their prayer. It shows that their humble dependence on God was met with a real response.
entries.8:24: Ezra set apart twelve leading priests, along with Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brothers. He chose trusted men to take charge of the valuable offerings.
entries.8:25: Ezra handed over the silver, gold, and temple vessels that had been donated for God's house. This shows careful handling of gifts meant for worship.
entries.8:26: He weighed out large amounts of silver and gold into their hands. Weighing it shows the value was carefully measured and accounted for.
entries.8:27: He also gave them gold basins and fine bronze vessels worth as much as gold. These valuable items were part of the offering for God's house.
entries.8:28: Ezra told these men that they and the vessels were set apart for the Lord, and that the silver and gold were a freewill offering to God. It reminds the reader that what is given to God is holy and must be treated with care.
entries.8:29: Ezra told them to guard everything until they could weigh it out in Jerusalem before the priests, Levites, and family leaders. It shows the importance of honesty and accountability with what belongs to God.
entries.8:30: The priests and Levites accepted the weighed silver, gold, and vessels to carry them to God's house in Jerusalem. They took on the responsibility of transporting holy things safely.
entries.8:31: They left the river on the twelfth day of the first month and traveled to Jerusalem, and God protected them from enemies along the way. It shows that their trust in God was rewarded with safe travel.
entries.8:32: When they arrived in Jerusalem, they rested for three days. This simple detail shows the journey was completed and they took time to recover.
entries.8:33: On the fourth day, the silver, gold, and vessels were weighed out in God's house and handed to trusted priests and Levites. It shows the gifts were delivered and accounted for exactly as planned.
entries.8:34: Everything was checked by number and weight, and the amounts were written down at that time. This shows careful record-keeping so nothing was lost or misused.
entries.8:35: The returned exiles offered burnt offerings and sin offerings to the God of Israel. It shows they began their new life in the land by worshiping God and seeking forgiveness.
entries.8:36: They delivered the king's orders to the royal officials and governors in the region, and those leaders gave support to the people and God's house. It shows the king's decree helped the returned community get the help they needed.
entries.9:1: The leaders told Ezra that the returned exiles, including priests, had intermarried with the surrounding peoples and adopted their detestable practices. It means God's people had blurred the line between faith and the culture around them, and the reader is warned that compromise often starts at the top.
entries.9:2: They had married foreign women, mixing the holy people with the surrounding nations, and the leaders were the worst offenders. It means those with the most responsibility set the bad example, so readers should be careful that their own influence doesn't lead others astray.
entries.9:3: Ezra was so devastated by the report that he tore out his hair and beard and sat down stunned. It means real grief over sin is physical and honest, and the reader is invited to take sin seriously rather than shrug it off.
entries.9:4: Everyone who trembled at God's word gathered around Ezra, and he sat there appalled until the evening sacrifice. It means those who honor God's word will be drawn together in shared concern, and the reader can find comfort in not grieving alone.
entries.9:5: At the evening sacrifice Ezra got up from his humiliation and knelt with hands spread out to God. It means prayer is the right response to a crisis, and the reader can bring heavy situations to God openly and humbly.
entries.9:6: Ezra was too ashamed to look up, confessing that the people's sins had piled up beyond their heads and reached heaven. It means sin is serious and needs honest confession, and the reader is encouraged to name their wrongs plainly before God.
entries.9:7: From their ancestors' days until now the people had sinned greatly, and their sins had brought defeat, captivity, plunder, and disgrace. It means sin has real consequences that can last generations, and the reader is reminded to learn from the past rather than repeat it.
entries.9:8: God had shown brief grace by letting a remnant return and giving them a firm foothold in his holy place, bringing light and renewed life. It means God's mercy gives fresh starts even after failure, and the reader can look for God's kindness in hard times.
entries.9:9: Though still servants, God had not abandoned them in their bondage but showed mercy before the Persian kings, enabling them to rebuild his house and giving them a wall in Judah and Jerusalem. It means God can work through powerful outsiders to help his people, and the reader can trust that God is present even in difficult circumstances.
entries.9:10: Ezra asks what can be said now, since the people had failed to keep God's commands. It means there are no excuses left for disobedience, and the reader is invited to be honest about their own failures instead of defending them.
entries.9:11: God had told them through the prophets that the land was unclean because of the detestable practices of its peoples. It means God had warned them clearly in advance, and the reader is reminded that God's warnings are meant to protect, not to spoil.
entries.9:12: God had commanded them not to intermarry or seek the peace and prosperity of these peoples, so that they could be strong and pass the land to their children. It means loyalty to God matters more than convenient alliances, and the reader should guard their closest commitments.
entries.9:13: Ezra acknowledges that their punishment was less than their sins deserved and that God had spared a remnant from death. It means God's discipline is mixed with mercy, and the reader can be grateful that God does not treat us as our sins deserve.
entries.9:14: Ezra asks whether they should again break God's commands by marrying into these peoples, which would bring total destruction with no survivors. It means repeating known sin invites serious consequences, and the reader is warned not to presume on God's patience.
entries.9:15: Ezra confesses that God is righteous while they are a spared remnant standing before him in guilt, and no one can stand on their own merit. It means we depend entirely on God's mercy, and the reader is pointed toward humility rather than self-justification.
entries.10:1: Ezra was praying and openly admitting the people's wrong, crying and lying down in front of God's house. A large crowd of men, women, and children gathered around him, all weeping bitterly, showing how deeply the sin had hurt the community.
entries.10:2: Shecaniah spoke up and admitted that the people had sinned against God by marrying women from the surrounding peoples. Even so, he said there was still hope for Israel, showing that confession can open the door to change.
entries.10:3: Shecaniah proposed making a solemn promise to God to send away these wives and their children, if Ezra and the others who respected God's word agreed, and to do it according to the law. This was a serious step to correct a serious wrong.
entries.10:4: Shecaniah urged Ezra to take action, promising that the people would stand behind him. He encouraged Ezra to be strong and get the job done, since it was his responsibility to lead.
entries.10:5: Ezra stood up and made the leading priests, the Levites, and all Israel swear an oath to carry out this plan. They agreed and bound themselves by that promise.
entries.10:6: Ezra left the area in front of God's house and went into a room belonging to Jehohanan. He ate and drank nothing there because he was still grieving over the sin of the returned exiles.
entries.10:7: A public notice went out through all Judah and Jerusalem telling everyone who had returned from exile to gather in Jerusalem.
entries.10:8: Anyone who failed to show up within three days would lose all his property and be excluded from the community of returned exiles, as the leaders had decided. This showed how serious the matter was.
entries.10:9: Within the three days, the men of Judah and Benjamin gathered in Jerusalem on the twentieth day of the ninth month. They sat in the open square before God's house, trembling because of the issue at hand and because of heavy rain.
entries.10:10: Ezra stood up and told the people plainly that they had sinned by marrying foreign women, which added to Israel's guilt. He named the wrong directly rather than softening it.
entries.10:11: Ezra called the people to confess to the Lord, the God of their ancestors, and to do what pleased him. Specifically, they were to separate themselves from the surrounding peoples and from these foreign wives.
entries.10:12: The whole assembly answered in a loud voice, agreeing that Ezra was right and that they should do as he said.
entries.10:13: The people pointed out that there were too many of them, it was raining heavily, and they could not stand outside any longer. They also noted that this problem was too big to settle in a day or two because their sin was great.
entries.10:14: They suggested that their leaders act on behalf of everyone, and that those in each town who had married foreign women come at scheduled times with the town's elders and judges. This would continue until God's fierce anger over the matter was turned away.
entries.10:15: Only Jonathan and Jahzeiah opposed this plan, and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite backed them up. So the proposal did not have unanimous support.
entries.10:16: The returned exiles carried out the plan. Ezra and chosen heads of families, listed by name, were set apart, and on the first day of the tenth month they began carefully investigating the matter.
entries.10:17: By the first day of the first month they had finished dealing with all the men who had married foreign women. The process took about three months to complete.
entries.10:18: Among the priests who had married foreign women were men from the family of Jeshua son of Jozadak, along with his brothers: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah.
entries.10:19: These men pledged to send their wives away, and to make things right for their sin they offered a ram from the flock as a guilt offering.
entries.10:20: From the family of Immer, the men involved were Hanani and Zebadiah.
entries.10:21: From the family of Harim, the men listed were Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah.
entries.10:22: From the family of Pashhur, the men named were Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah.
entries.10:23: Among the Levites, the men listed were Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah (also called Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer.
entries.10:24: Among the singers, Eliashib was named, and among the gatekeepers, Shallum, Telem, and Uri.
entries.10:25: From the rest of Israel, the family of Parosh included Ramiah, Izziah, Malchijah, Mijamin, Eleazar, Malchijah, and Benaiah.
entries.10:26: From the family of Elam, the men named were Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi, Jeremoth, and Elijah.
entries.10:27: From the family of Zattu, the men listed were Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad, and Aziza.
entries.10:28: From the family of Bebai, the men named were Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai.
entries.10:29: From the family of Bani, the men listed were Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Jeremoth.
entries.10:30: From the family of Pahath-moab, the men named were Adna, Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezalel, Binnui, and Manasseh.
entries.10:31: From another branch of the family of Harim, the men listed were Eliezer, Isshijah, Malchijah, Shemaiah, and Shimeon.
entries.10:32: Also from that group were Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah.
entries.10:33: From the family of Hashum, the men named were Mattenai, Mattattah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei.
entries.10:34: From the family of Bani, the men listed were Maadai, Amram, and Uel.
entries.10:35: Continuing that list were Benaiah, Bedeiah, and Cheluhi.
entries.10:36: Also named were Vaniah, Meremoth, and Eliashib.
entries.10:37: The list continues with Mattaniah, Mattenai, and Jaasu.
entries.10:38: Also included were Bani, Binnui, and Shimei.
entries.10:40: The list ends with Machnadebai, Shashai, and Sharai.
entries.10:41: This verse just lists three more men by name among a larger group. It reminds the reader that these were real individuals, each counted in what the community was dealing with.
entries.10:42: Three more names are added to the same list. The point is simply that every person was named and accounted for, not lost in a crowd.
entries.10:43: This verse names a group of men from the family of Nebo. It continues the same record, showing that several families were involved in the same situation.
entries.10:44: These men had all married women from outside their people, and some of those marriages had produced children. It shows the situation was serious and had real family consequences, not just a rule being broken.
